story_text.value:
Hello everyone,

I am Elie a CS student in Switzerland, and for the past 3 months I've been building Swingback, a user feedback platform, with voting, Github/Linear integrations, and much more.

I started building this app as I was working on another project of mine and got really frustrated about the price and lack of features of the other platform (pay-per-user, no integration with Github, no translation, ...). So I've decided to go on (a much longer that I care to admit) sidequest building what is, for me, the perfect feedback platform.

Swingback has a free plan that you can use and will not stop people giving feedback (some of my competitors, for example, do not allow auto-signin (user being directly sing-in when opening the feedback tab), which add friction to people who wants to give feedback). There is also a paid plan, which include more integrations, removing the branding and other goodies.

It would mean the world if you guys would give Swingback a try. You can also check the Swingback feedback portal (https://feedback.swingback.dev) to see what feature are coming ;)

Best, Elie (aka Fayorg) https://eliebaier.ch

title.value: Show HN: Swingback, get feedback from your user for free

story_text.value:
I made a tool to show how much revenue declined cards are costing your SaaS.

You make a read-only Stripe key, and it totals every subscription invoice from the last 90 days that was attempted, failed, and never paid. Plus what Stripe's retries already recovered.

Key is used once and never stored.

I worked a lot with cloc, sloc and scc and used them in various prohects. But with AI driven development some of the models COCOMO I and II might not be applicable.

So built a new cli ccm short for code counter machine with new calculation model which estimate the new AI driven development costs. The formula, logic and the estimates used are there in the docs.

Documentation: https://insanai.github.io/ccm/

story_text.value:
To tackle the ever-increasing number of tests, I built cargo-test-prune.

The idea behind it is to use cargo-mutants to generate mutants, and then solve the set cover problem for those mutants to suggest which tests can be eliminated. (use a greedy algorithm to cover the detected mutants with fewer tests)

I came up with this as a countermeasure against the monotonically increasing tests that tend to accumulate, especially when coding with AI.

In fact, this very repository was also written using AI.

I ran this tool on a previous revision of this repository. There were 11 tests and 108 generated mutants: 73 were caught by the tests, 23 survived, and 12 failed to compile. I removed the 5 tests suggested by the tool and re-ran the same 108 mutants. The remaining 6 tests caught the exact same 73 mutants.

Tests partly serve as documentation, so simply applying this isn't necessarily recommended, but since writing less code still holds value in the AI era, I think this tool could be quite useful.

title.value: Show HN: Find overlapping Rust tests with mutation testing
